I've been farming my 220 mu in Quzhou County for five years now. With my education, I follow the county extension office's advice but I also keep a close eye on costs and what has worked on my land. My system is spring soybean, but I grow millet too because it handles dry spells better and the grain price has been stable.

This season, I will plant **100 mu of millet** and **120.1 mu of spring soybean**. I will buy improved varieties from the county seed station — they are proven here and cheaper than hybrids. I will use rotary tillage for both crops; it is fast and leaves a fine seedbed that works well with my well-irrigation setup.

For fertilizer, millet is a heavy feeder so I will give it **10 kg of nitrogen per mu**, plus **5 kg phosphorus** and **4 kg potassium**. Soybean fixes its own nitrogen, so I will only apply **4 kg nitrogen per mu** to get it started, but **5 kg phosphorus and 3 kg potassium** to support root nodulation and pod filling. 

Pumping water costs electricity, so I will irrigate smartly. Millet will get **three irrigations**: at sowing, at jointing, and at heading. Soybean only needs **two**: at sowing and at flowering. For pesticides, **two sprays** on each crop will be enough to control aphids and any pod borers without wasting money on too many chemicals.

I expect **250 kg per mu from the millet** and **180 kg per mu from the soybean**. These targets match what I have achieved the last couple of years with this level of management.
